script: My boyfriend demanded an abortion—now I am 7 months pregnant, wedding looming.. I was 32, white, living my best life, when my 28‑year‑old Indian boyfriend—yeah, the guy who'd fought like a champ to make us a thing—hit me with the ultimate bomb: "Get an abortion before we tie the knot." He's got a big wedding planned for the end of January, more than 450 people, family, friends, the whole she‑bang. We're about to be a couple in a big cultural mash‑up, and he's terrified of the fallout if he's got a baby before the big day. He's saying if it was a few months later, we'd just be celebrating. (Micro‑hook: "If it was a few months later, we'd just be celebrating.") I am white, he's Indian. We've had the whole "not the same culture" drama, but we fought through it. He's the love of my life, my best friend, the one who makes my heart skip. But this—this pregnancy—feels like a weight that could crush us both. (Stakes: I am pregnant, he's scared of family disowning him, I am terrified of the health risks, we're about to lose a huge event, and my own body is a battleground.) I've been trying to get pregnant for years. Six years in a past relationship, nothing. Two years with him, still nothing. I checked my AMH—low, like 1.0—so I did egg freezing. First round, I got two eggs. Second round, I ovulated early (like 0.5% of the time), they cancelled the retrieval. I left the clinic feeling like I'd hit a dead end. Then, out of nowhere, I got pregnant. (Micro‑hook: "Then, out of nowhere, I got pregnant.") I've got a history of estrogen‑related breast cancer. The hormones needed for a pregnancy could be a nightmare. I am also Rh‑negative, so there's the whole Rh sensitivity drama. The medical stuff is scary, but the emotional stakes are higher. I am not a pessimist; I know I could get pregnant again, but it might be a Herculean task. (Stakes: My health, potential future pregnancies, my emotional well‑being.) He's saying that if I keep the baby, I am "killing people" with the news, that he'd be "selfish and manipulative," and that I'd ruin his life. He's terrified of his family disowning him. He's saying he can't cancel the wedding because of reputation, because he fought for us. (Stakes: His family, our wedding, our future together.) If I go through with an abortion, I don't know if I'll ever look at myself in the mirror and see the same person. If I don't, I feel like I am letting him down, like I am playing with his life. (Open loop: "If I don't, I feel like I am letting him down.") The options feel like a death‑match: 1. Stay together, no abortion. He feels trapped, I feel like I am compromising myself. 2. Stay together, abortion. He feels betrayed, I feel my soul ripped from my body. 3. Break up, single mom. I have no clue how I'd survive financially or physically. 4. Break up, abortion. The whole world I know is ripped away. I can't see my life without him, but I can't live with the decision to end everything I've hoped for. (Tension wave: short punchy lines, then longer reflection.) I am looking for a third path, a way that doesn't mean killing a baby, doesn't mean tearing us apart, and doesn't mean losing my own sense of self. I am not asking for a miracle; I am asking for a plan that respects both our lives, our cultures, and our future. (Clarity: "I am not asking for a miracle; I am asking for a plan that respects both our lives.")
